implementation_notes: sqlx derives row-to-struct mapping and, with #[sqlx(flatten)], a field that itself implements FromRow is parsed with its own implementation instead of as a single column - the documented example reads id, name, country, city, road into a User whose address is an Address. That is the recompose half of the pattern generated from the type definitions; the write half is the ordinary query with one bind parameter per field. Note the attribute's limit: it flattens by field name, so the value's column names must match its fields (use rename_all or explicit rename on the nested type) and the flat field itself must not correspond to a column.
pitfalls: flatten reads the nested type's field names verbatim from the row, so a value type whose field names differ from the column names needs rename/rename_all on the nested struct, not on the owner.

If the value's type is not decodable from the returned columns the error surfaces at runtime as a column-not-found, not at compile time - unlike Diesel, sqlx does not check the query against the type.
A flattened field cannot also be read as a single column: the same type must not implement both a scalar Decode and the flattened FromRow for the same query.

variants.name: Diesel #[diesel(embed)] with a Selectable value type
variants.idiom_name: #[diesel(embed)] on a value struct deriving Selectable/Queryable
variants.implementation_notes: Diesel maps query results to Rust types per query rather than per table, and #[diesel(embed)] is its documented way to nest one type inside another: the attribute declares that the field maps not to a single database field but to a struct that maps to several, and Selectable then builds a nested select clause from it. The flattening is therefore checked at compile time - field count, order and SQL types must line up - which is the opposite trade-off to sqlx's runtime column lookup: more safety, noisier compile errors, and the same value type must be reused consistently across the queries that select it.
pitfalls: The select clause must line up with the struct field by field; adding a field to the value type changes the expected column list and breaks every query that selects it, at compile time.
The order of fields, not just their names, is part of the mapping, so reordering a struct's fields silently changes which column is read into which field unless check_for_backend is enabled.
The same value type must be selectable from each table that embeds it; a value shared across tables needs the columns to be named identically or a per-query select_expression.
